This portion of the outline relies heavily upon the material from Tom Valletta and in chapter one of Richard Bushman's Joseph Smith and the Beginnings of Mormonism. When direct quotes are used, reference will be noted. Other sources are also used and appropriately referenced. 1. Narrative of Lucy hack Smith the central source for Family Background a) Lucy began her work just six months after martyrdom b) Martha Jane Knowlton Coray, a Nauvoo schoolteacher, recorded Lucy Smith's narrative in a series of notebooks (1) From these notes, a preliminary manuscript was prepared (2) Coray and Lucy Smith further revised the manuscript (3) Orson Pratt published it in Liverpool in 1853 with Lucy's permission c) Brigham Young appointed a committee to correct inaccuracies and make other editorial changes (1) This version was published as History of the Prophet Joseph Smith, revised by George A. Smith and Elias Smith in 1902 (2) A later edition was based on the 1902 edition and published as History of Joseph Smith bv His Mother. Lucy Mack Smith [Edited and with notes and commentary by Preston Nibley, 1958.] d) The Smith family as a whole, rather than Joseph Smith, was the central theme of her book (!) Joseph is not even mentioned until page 56 In the course of relating family moves she adds, almost parenthetically, "in the meantime we had a son, whom we called Joseph, after the name of his father; he was born December 23, 1805. I shall speak of him more particularly by and by." (p. 56.] (2) Her narrative begins with her father (Solomon) and she devotes five chapters about family before getting to herself 2. Joseph Smith, Jr. Family History (1) Robert Smith (a) Born in Toppefield Co., Essex, England (b) Was fifteen when he sailed from England in 1638 at the height of the Puritan migration and ended up in Topsfield (c) Died wealthy-£189 (2) Samuel Smith (a) Born 26 Jan. 1666 (b) Held many public offices (3) Captain Samuel Smith (a) Born 27 Jan. 1714 in Topsfield. Mass. (b) Active at the Boston Tea Party-chairman of the Tea committee, in 1773 (c) Many honors heaped upon him from the town i) Repeatedly chose assessor, selectman, town clerk, representative to the General Court and delegate to the Provincial Congress ii) He was chose twenty times as moderator of the town meeting, a position reserved for one who commanded universal respect iii) During Revolution he served on the Committee of Safety fv) When he died November 14, 1785, his obituary stated that he: "was esteemed a man of integrity and uprightness.... a sincere mend to the liberties or his country, and a strenuous advocate For the doctrines of Christianity." [Bushman, p. 20.J (4) Asael Smith "01 crooked neck" (a) Born 7 March 1744 in Topsfield, Mass. (b) Asael's mother died when he was six months old (c) His mother's cousin married his father a year later-she did not treat him kindly, From his reports (d) As the youngest of five children, there was not much of an inheritance from Samuel (e) In 1767, at age twenty-three, Asael married Mary Duty (f) For five years they lived with Samuel and his second wife Priscilla (g) In May, 1772, Asael moved with wife and three children to Windham, New Hampshire, where Mary's family had migrated (h) Two years later Asael and Mary were a few miles north in Dunbarlon on the Merrimack River (!) In summer of 1776 Asael enlisted for a few months' service along the northern New York frontier (j) During the early years of the Revolution the family was probably in Salem, New Hampshire (k) In 1777, when the sixth child was born, Asael was thirty-three and still in search of a place to sink his roots. (I) in 1778 Asael and Mary purchased 100 acres on the Merrimack River and opened a coopering business (m) A year after acquiring property in Derryfieid, Asael was elected town clerk (n) When his father died, he took over the farm and moved his wife and 10 children into Topsfieid (o) For five years Asael raised cattle and sheep for the market and grain, potatoes, vegetables, and fruit for the family (p) To pay the debts incurred by his father, Asael sold the farm (q) They also sold the Topsfield property in 1791 and purchased eighty-three acres of uncleared land in Tunbridge, Vermont, for £26 (r) Each of Asael's four married children bore him a grandchild in 1799. Moved by this fact he composed at age fifty-five: (See handout entitled "Asael Smith's Address To His Family.") (s) Between 1511 and 1820 Asael and Mary and at least seven of the eleven children moved from Tunbridge i) Six of the seven settled around their parents once again, this time in Stockholm and Potsdam in St. Lawrence Co., New York ii) They presumably all worked together in opening up new farms (t) By 1802, the Smiths had a 300-400-acre compound of adjoining farms (u) Asael was elected three times as a selectman of Tunbridge (one of the three active men chose to look after the town's affairs) (v) During a visit of Lucy with her brother Stephen, she met Asael's second son, Joseph (w) Most of Asael's family were living close together in 1828 when Joseph Smith, Sr., wrote the news of the visions of his son i) In 1830 he came personally with copies of the Book of Mormon ii) Asael and Mary and three of the four surviving sons and all but two daughters believed the teachings of the restoration iii) Only Jesse, the eldest, held back from the church iv) In 1836 the clan, excluding Asael, who died in 1830, gathered in Kirtland-Mary Duty was with them "Of the thirteen members of the Asael Smith family, seven accepted the Mormon faith, three died before they had an opportunity, and three rejected it. John Smith, who was baptized in 1832, was the first to Join the church." [Bushman, p. 198n.J v) At the end of the 500-mile journey Joseph, Jr., and Hyrum met their ninety-two-year-old grandmother in her Fairport hotel room "Joseph blessed here and said she was the most honored woman on earth." Richard Lloyd Anderson, Joseph Smith's New England Heritage, p. 111-116. (x) Asael gave more religious direction to his family than did Solomon Mack, whose conversion did not occur until late in life i) Asael's father saw to the baptism of all his four children in the Topsfield Congregational church ii) At eighteen Asael was assigned a seat in the meetinghouse, and in 1772 husband and wife owned the covenant "Owning the covenant did not make them full members of the church. One had to show evidence of supernatural grace and have an assurance of salvation before becoming a voting member. Owning the covenant meant that they believed the doctrines outlined in the covenant and promised to live an upright and moral life. That degree of commitment allowed them to present Jesse, Joseph, and Priscilla for baptism." [Bushman, p. 26.J iii) The absence of assurance of divine grace did not mean that Asael and Mary lacked religious convictions (1) In eighteenth century puritanism, dissenters from strict Calvinist orthodoxy justified their departures on the basis of reason (2) A group of Harvard-educated ministers argued that Calvinism read ideas into the scripture (a) They argued that it was unscriptural and dangerous to believe that God saved men arbitrarily (b) They asked, what good were human strivings? (c) Their reasoning brought men back to the ideas of Jacobus Arminius, who raised similar objection to Calvinism in the 17th cent. (3) This reasonable spirit was in the air when Asael Smith began forming his beliefs (a) Reason freed him from an unthinking acceptance of traditional teachings (b) He did not opt for Arminianism, but instead leaned toward the Universalist teachings of John Murray i) John Murray arrived in America from England in 1770 and settled in Gloucester. Mass, ii) Not Boston-born nor Harvard-bred, his teachings were more widely accepted by the common people than the Arminians iii) He taught that Christ assumed the sins of all men and redeemed them all by his atonement iv) Men did not merit grace by their good works v) Christ's grace alone redeemed them, but it was powerful enough to redeem everyone without exception vi) Murray carried the Calvinist idea of irresistible grace to its logical conclusion (4) Because of Vermont's common unorthodoxy, it became the focus of intense missionary efforts-revivals became common after 1801 (5) The revivals had a strong effect on the family, causing them to become more orthodox (6) Of all the children, only Joseph remained aloof from conventional religion (5) Joseph smith, Sr. (a) Born 12 July 1771 in Topsfield, Mass. His reason for writing was to show that God had repeatedly humbled him and showed him the vanity of the world, and yet he had remained blind and deaf to the Lord's call. These two could not be absent at an assumption of power, since it was the Nbty, the Two Ladies, from whom the King received his office. Hathor was Isis, whose name simply means throne, leading to never-ending speculation as to just how literally such things were to be taken; while Maat was the double of Wrr.t, the Great Lady, the Crown itself--again, was she the crown? This swapping of the sexes back and forth is found among our own ancestors of not so long ago as the couvade, the purpose of which was to give both father and mother equal claim on the heirs. Perhaps the neatest bull's eye that the Prophet Joseph makes in the Explanations, is in designating Figure 5 in Facsimile No. 3 as "Shulem, one of King(s principal waiters." Wherever did he get that idea? Nobody ever heard of Shulem, who is never mentioned anywhere else, before or after, in our story. Indeed. it seems that nothing in Smith's interpretation of this Facsimile is as the normal candid observer would see it. The figure standing in the center of the picture with upraised hands should be Abraham discoursing on astronomy, while the man on the throne should certainly be Pharaoh, and the two ladies (which any three-year old would point out to you as females without a moment's hesitation) might be Pharaoh's wife and daughter--or perhaps Figure 4 could even be Sarah, introducing her husband to the King, while Abraham's colored servant, Eleaser, stands behind him. Almost anything is more reasonable than what Joseph Smith has given us! But if we consult the court scenes on other biographical or autobiographical records, we soon learn that the man standing in the center of the picture is almost always the owner of the stele, what is more that he is usually some personal servant or palace officer attendant on Pharaoh. From the collection of H. R. Hall we go down the list of "Chief of Bowmen...Fan-bearer, King's Messenger, Treasury Guard, King's Chief Charioteer, Pharaoh's Chief Boatman, Warden of the Harem, the Queen's Chief Cook," etc., etc. They were simply servants. but to serve in the most menial capacity in close personal and intimate attendance on the King has ever been considered an appointment devoutly to be wished for. Some of the officials. e.g., the King's Chief Charioteer, bore good Canaanite names, and so does "Shulem, one of the King's Principal Waiters" (p.161). How naturally he fits into the picture! This is his show and this is his document. It seems to recall the time when he was introduced by the Pharaoh to an illustrious fellow- countrymen whom the King was honoring as a great and famous visiting teacher. Why do we depend on Shulem for our information? M. Gemoll gives us a clue for he notes that the best way for Abraham to have preserved his record after he had moved back to Palestine, would be to leave it reposing safely in an Egyptian tomb. The Joseph Smith Papyri were found preserved in the vaults of a priestly family of Thebes among many documents dating from different times. "I will not say who these people were," wrote the Prophet of their ancient owners, though he denied that the mummies were those of Biblical characters, and identified one princess by the perfectly good Egyptian name of Ka-tu-men, as having lived a thousand years after Abraham. No one has explained more fully or, in view of much modern research more accurately than Joseph Smith the manner in which ancient records were transmitted through many hands, with much editing, abridging, re-copying, commentating, deletion and addition; and how some were deliberately sealed and hidden away "to come forth in their purity." Joseph had constantly to restrain the enthusiasm of his followers in Kirtland in leaping to romantic and quite unjustified conclusions regarding the papyri--as LDS students still do. But he himself never goes out of bound. As far-fetched as his Explanations once appeared, and still do appear to those not bothering to look beyond the superficial aspect of things, they can at the very least be held up at plausible to those who are inclined to search farther. A. unusual excitement This excitement is best outlined in Milt Backman's Joseph Smith's First Vision (pp.53-89). There were so many revivals that the area was called the "burned-over district". 1. The churches kept the questions of salvation before the settler; there were four churches within a few miles of the Smith's a) Presbyterians had the largest congregation In Palmyra village and In 1820 had the only meetinghouse b) The Methodists were second largest, and constructed a building of their own in 1822 c) The Society of Fiends built their meetingplace in 1823 d) Just two miles west of the village a large congregation of Baptists met in a meetinghouse of their own since 1808 e) In the eastern part of Palmyra stood a second Presbyterian church 2. Revivals had appeared periodically from 1799 on. touching one town and then another a) Over one hundred people joined the Baptist church in Palmyra during a revival in 1808, making a new chapel necessary b) The great revival of 1816 and 1817 in Palmyra doubled the number of Presbyterians and led to the forming of a new congregation (1) This revival had a powerful effect on both Joseph, Sr. and Lucy who were concerned about salvation (2) Joseph, Jr. also began to be concerned about religion "at about the age of twelve years'-this would be late 1817 or early 1818 [See 1832 Recital of the First Vision in Handout] c) In July, 1819, the Methodists of the Genesee Conference met for a week in Vienna, about 13 miles from the Smith Farm (1) The Manchester Baptists increased their numbers 25 percent (2) The Geneva Presbytery, which included churches in Joseph's immediate area, reported in February, 1820 that: "during the past year more have been received into the communion of the Churches than perhaps in any former year." (See Milton Backman, Jr., pp. 79-89. Backman presents extensive evidence that their were extensive revivals matching Joseph's description of the time.] (3) This may have been some of the "unusual excitement" which affected "the whole district of country" and caused "no small stir" [SeeJS-H 1:5] (4) At an unspecified date, Lucy overcame her reservations and joined the Western Presbyterian Church in Palmyra (5) Hyrum, Sophronia, and Samuel joined with her; but Joseph Smith, Sr. and the other sons held back (6) Joseph Smith, Jr., "became somewhat partial to the Methodist sect," and came close to joining, but also held back (a) Two printer's apprentices at the Palmyra Register who knew Joseph remembered his Methodist leanings i) One said he caught "a spark of Methodism in the camp meeting, away down in the woods, on the Vienna road" ii) The other remembered that Joseph joined the probationary class of the Palmyra Methodist Church (b) Joseph later recounted "some desire to be united with them" (c) He said that "he wanted to get religion too, wanted to feel and shout like the rest but could feel nothing" (7) Joseph felt like the revivals led to much division {See JS-H 1: 6] 3. Joseph's personal struggle with religion a) His mother remembered Joseph as a "remarkably quiet, well-disposed child" b) Lucy described him as "much less inclined to the perusal of books than the rest of our children, but far more given bo meditation and deep study." (Lucy Smith, pp. 73, 64.] c) Between the ages of twelve and fifteen he seriously searched the scriptures. "believing as I was taught, that they contained the word of God." [Lucy Smith, p. 04.] d) Joseph had at least two questions in his mind: (1) Which church was right (2) How to be saved e) His anguish for himself mingled with his anguish for the world, for the corruption in the churches seemed to obscure salvation: "From the age of twelve years to fifteen I pondered many things in my heart concerning the situation of the world of mankind; the contentions and divisions; the wickedness and abominations and the darkness which pervaded the minds of mankind. My mind became exceedingly distressed for I became convicted of my sins and by searching the scriptures I found that mankind did not come unto the Lord but that they had apostatized from the true and living faith. And there was no society or denomination that built upon the Gospel of Jesus Christ as recorded in the New Testament and I felt to mourn for my own sins and for the sins of the world." [Joseph Smith. "History of the Life of Joseph Smith, Jr.." p. 156. (Known as the 1832 Account)) f) Joseph even attended the meetings of a "juvenile debating club," which met In the red school house on Durfee Street Orasmus Turner, one of theological newspaper apprentices, said Joseph came to the club to solve some portentous questions of moral or political ethics." Perhaps Joseph followed the precedent of rationally debating some of the classic arguments of God and religion. Years later, Oliver Cowdery said that Joseph wondered for a time whether "a Supreme Being did exist," but rested his faith on the beauty of the created universe. {Bushman, pp. 55.J g) In this state of inner struggle and confusion Joseph kept studying the scriptures and finally was struck by James 1:5 t SeeJS-H 1: 10-12.] h) "At length I came to the conclusion that I must either remain in darkness and confusion, or else I must do as James directs..." US-H 1: 13.]

words.meaning: in Hebrew. According to Gesenius there are four meanings to the word rectitude or being right, justice, piety or virtue, and welfare. However, the one definition that gets the most play in Nauvoo is the final meaning - welfare. In the same issue of the Times and Seasons which printed this account of the First Vision is Rabbi Hersch's article where is righteousness is defined as "when applied to God, denotes his charitable righteousness, which gives to man. not that which he deserves, but that which he can bear: so. when applied to man it denotes that charitable righteousness which makes the love of God, rather than the right of another, the ground of assisting him." Times and Seasons (Times and Seasons Vol. 3 pp.726, printed March 15, 1842). In essence. Rabbi Hersh ties righteousness to charity. Charity is a gift that comes from above (see Moroni 7:48). Therefore, righteousness 'is sent down from heaven' to gather in the elect.

quotes.text: The Lord has declared, "He that feareth me shall be looking forth for the great day of the Lord to come, even for the signs of the coming of the Son of Man," signs that will be shown "in the heavens above, and in the earth beneath" (D&C 45:39-40). The Savior taught this in the parable of the fig tree whose tender new branches give a sign of the coming of summer. "So likewise," when the elect shall see the signs of His coming, "they shall know that he is near, even at the doors" (Joseph Smith-Matthew 1:38-39; see also Matthew 24:32-33; D&C 45:37-38). Biblical and modern prophecies give many signs of the Second Coming. These include: 1. The fulness of the gospel restored and preached in all the world for a witness to all nations. 2. False Christs and false prophets, deceiving many. 3. Wars and rumors of wars, with nation rising against nation. 4. Earthquakes in divers places. 5. Famine and pestilence. 6. An overflowing scourge, a desolating sickness covering the land. 7. Iniquity abounding. 8. The whole earth in commotion. 9. Men's hearts failing them. (See Matthew 24:5-15; Joseph Smith-Matthew 1:22, 28-32; D&C 45:26-33.)
quotes.speaker: Dallin H. Oaks
quotes.attr: Dallin H. Oaks, in Conference Report, Apr. 2004, 5; or Ensign, May 2004, 7

quotes.text: Keith W. Perkins, chairman of the department of Church History and Doctrine at BYU, said that the JST teaches a truth about the Second Coming "that is found nowhere else in scripture," and "which has not only been ignored by biblical scholars but also has been almost entirely overlooked by Latter-day Saints." JST Luke 12:41-42 refers to Christ's coming in the first, second, and third watches of the night-indicating that although "there will be an actual time when Christ will return to earth again to greet those in the flesh who are so privileged to meet Him in that day," Christ comes "in every watch of the night." In other words, "no preparation that we make for the Second Coming of Christ is in vain, for in effect he comes in every generation." For example, if we die prior to his coming, the joy of our reunion with him "will be just the same as if we were living on the earth when he finally does return in great glory. … With this knowledge may we not worry so much about the day of his coming, but rather about our preparation to meet him regardless of the day.
quotes.speaker: Marvin K. Gardner
quotes.attr: Marvin K. Gardner, "News of the Church," Ensign, Jan. 1985, 77

quotes.text: On another day in another place, however, the sun was setting on the mortal ministry of the Messiah as he departed the temple at Jerusalem for the last time. Climbing atop the Mount of Olives with his disciples, the Savior prophesied the cataclysmic events that would precede the destruction of Jerusalem and his second coming. He then issued this portentous admonition to his disciples, ancient and modern: “Then you shall stand in the holy place; whoso readeth let him understand” (Joseph Smith—Matthew 1:12; italics added; see also Matthew 24:15). Latter-day revelations provide understanding. They teach that in our day, amidst strife and catastrophe and pestilence, there are two kingdoms locked in grim struggle for the souls of men—Zion and Babylon. More than once they repeat the injunction to “stand in holy places” for a refuge from these storms of latter-day life (D&C 45:32; see also D&C 87:8; 101:16–23). Prominent among such holy places, and key to all the others, is the temple of the Lord.
quotes.speaker: Lance B. Wickman
quotes.attr: Lance B. Wickman, in Conference Report, Oct. 1994, 110; or Ensign, Nov. 1994, 82–83

quotes.text: Known as "Joseph Smith-Matthew" in the Pearl of Great Price, the JST of Matthew 24 is invaluable in bringing home the message and meaning of this remarkable sermon by the Savior to His Apostles. The order of the verses is changed to reflect the Lord's response to the disciples' two questions: "When shall these things [concerning the destruction of Jerusalem] be? and what shall be the sign of thy coming, at the end of the world?" (Matt. 24:3). His answer to the first question is found in JS-M 1:5-20; the answer to the second question is given in JS-M 1:21-55. In fact, the Prophet wrote an inspired transition that distinguishes between the time of Jerusalem's destruction and the time before the Savior's coming in glory: "Behold these things I have spoken unto you concerning the Jews; and again, after the tribulation of those days which shall come upon Jerusalem …" (JS-M 1:21; emphasis added). Thus, verse 21 marks the break between the time of Jerusalem's siege and the signs of the last days.
quotes.speaker: Ray L. Huntington and Camille Fronk
quotes.attr: Ray L. Huntington and Camille Fronk, "Latter-day Clarity on Christ's Life and Teachings," Ensign, Jan. 1999, 27

quotes.text: Matthew 24 as it stands in the Bible poses great problems for many readers in that the events of the destruction of the temple are intertwined with those preceding the Second Coming. The Prophet's revisions altered the order of several of the verses, thus making it plain that the Savior clearly answered both of the questions posed by his disciples. Verses 5 through 20 of Joseph Smith-Matthew answer the question of when the temple in Jerusalem would be destroyed and what would happen to the Jews, while verses 21 through 55 answer the question as to what shall be the signs of his Second Coming and the end of the world. For Latter-day Saints, the events leading up to the Second Coming are of primary interest. The emphasis of this chapter, read together with section 45 of the Doctrine and Covenants, is on our need to be prepared. In giving his Saints knowledge of the coming events, the Lord offers comfort, assuring us that despite fearsome trials and tribulations we may face, he is in charge.
quotes.speaker: David Rolph Seely
quotes.attr: David Rolph Seely, "The Joseph Smith Translation: 'Plain and Precious Things' Restored," Ensign, Aug. 1997, 15

quotes.text: As we have been counseled for more than 60 years, let us have some food set aside that would sustain us for a time in case of need. But let us not panic nor go to extremes…I cannot forget the great lesson of Pharaoh’s dream of the fat and lean kine and of the full and withered stalks of corn. I cannot dismiss from my mind the grim warnings of the Lord as set forth in the 24th chapter of Matthew. I am familiar, as are you, with the declarations of modern revelation that the time will come when the earth will be cleansed and there will be indescribable distress, with weeping and mourning and lamentation (see DC 112:24). Now I do not wish to be an alarmist. I do not wish to be a prophet of doom. I am optimistic. I do not believe the time is here when an all-consuming calamity will overtake us. I earnestly pray that it may not. There is so much of the Lord’s work yet to be done. We, and our children after us, must do it.
quotes.speaker: Gordon B. Hinckley
quotes.attr: Gordon B. Hinckley, Conference Report, Ensign, Oct. 2001, 73-74
